english: I drink coffee with a colleague.
tip: 랑 (rang) = with/and, casual: 동료랑 (dongnyorang = with a colleague).

english: I have so much to do today.
tip: 할 일 (hal il) is literally 'will-do work': 할 (hal) turns 하다 (hada = do) into a label for the noun after it. Korean builds 'things to do' straight from the verb.

english: I work at a bank.
tip: 다녀요 (danyeoyo), from 다니다 (danida = go regularly), is how Korean says you work somewhere: 은행에 다녀요 (eunhaeng-e danyeoyo) – showing up routinely IS the job.

english: I'm getting a lot of stress these days.
tip: 스트레스를 받아요 (seuteureseureul badayo) = 'receive stress' = to be stressed.

english: Where is the meeting room?
tip: 실 (sil) is a 'room' suffix: 회의실 (hoeuisil) = meeting room, 화장실 (hwajangsil) = bathroom. Spot the 실 and you know it's some kind of room.

english: We'll have lunch after the meeting.
tip: 후에 (hue = after) comes after its noun: 회의 후에 (hoeui hue) is literally 'meeting-after'. Korean time words trail the thing they anchor to – reversed from English.

english: Today's lunch is on me.
tip: 제가 사요 (jega sayo), 'I'm buying', is the standard offer to treat – 사다 (sada = buy) covers picking up the bill, no separate 'treat' verb needed.

english: On Fridays we have chicken and beer.
tip: 에 (e) can link food pairings: 치킨에 맥주 (chikin-e maekju) = chicken with beer. The combo is so beloved it compressed into one word, 치맥 (chimaek).

target: 이번 주에 야근을 세 번 했어요.
english: I worked late three times this week.
tip: 번 (beon) counts times, with native numbers: 세 번 (se beon = three times).

english: It's hard because there's so much work.
tip: 많아서 (manaseo) packs 'because there's a lot' into one word – the -아서 (-aseo) ending fuses the cause onto the verb, so no separate 'because' appears.

english: There's not much work today.
tip: 별로 (byeollo) + negative = not really: 별로 없어요 = not much.

english: Tomorrow is payday!
tip: 월급날 (wolgeumnal = payday) has a sound trap: it's spelled with ㅂ (b) before ㄴ (n), but ㅂ turns into ㅁ (m) there – say -mn-, never -pn-.

english: In the morning I shower and get dressed.
tip: -고 (go) links actions in order: 샤워하고 (syawohago = shower and then).

english: So I couldn't eat breakfast.
tip: 못 먹었어요 (mot meogeosseoyo) = couldn't eat: 못 (mot) means circumstances stopped you. 안 (an) would mean you chose to skip breakfast.

english: Good work again today.
tip: 수고했어요 (sugohaesseoyo) = 'you worked hard' — the everyday office goodbye.

english: I'm off first. See you tomorrow!
tip: 저 먼저 가요 (jeo meonjeo gayo) — the polite 'I'm leaving first' at the office.

target: 다음 주 금요일에 휴가를 쓸 거예요.
english: I'll use a vacation day next Friday.
tip: 휴가를 써요 (hyugareul sseoyo) = 'use' vacation days — 쓰다 means write AND use.

english: I live in an apartment.
tip: Most city Koreans live in 아파트 (apateu) — big high-rise complexes.

english: Our place is on the fifteenth floor.
tip: 층 (cheung) = floor, with Sino numbers: 십오 층 (sibo cheung = 15th floor).

english: There are two rooms.
tip: 개 (gae) = general counter, native numbers: 두 개 (du gae = two things).

english: I clean the house every weekend.
tip: 마다 (mada) sticks straight onto a noun: 주말마다 (jumal-mada) = every weekend. No extra particle needed – 마다 does 'every' all by itself.

english: I run the vacuum cleaner.
tip: Koreans 'spin' machines: 청소기를 돌려요 (cheongsogireul dollyeoyo = run the vacuum).

english: I washed the blankets.
tip: Korean picks the wash verb by what you wash – 빨다 (ppalda) is only for fabric: 이불을 빨았어요 (ibureul pparasseoyo). Dishes and your body take different verbs.

english: I watered the flowers.
tip: 물을 줘요 (mureul jwoyo) = 'give water' = to water plants.

english: I turn off the lights before bed.
tip: -기 전에 (gi jeone) = before doing: 자기 전에 (jagi jeone = before sleeping).

english: In Korea, people sort their recycling.
tip: 분리수거 (bullisugeo) = mandatory trash sorting — an apartment-life ritual.

english: I forgot the recycling yesterday.
tip: 깜빡했어요 (kkamppakaesseoyo) = 'it slipped my mind' — the spoken way to say you forgot to do something.

english: The delivery fee is 3,000 won.
tip: -비 (bi) = fee: 배달비 (baedalbi) = delivery fee.

english: Please leave it at the door.
tip: 놓아 주세요 (noa juseyo) ends in 주다 (juda = give) – adding it to a verb asks someone to do it as a favor for you: leave it at the door for me.

english: Today I want to eat something with broth.
tip: -고 싶어요 (go sipeoyo) = want to: 먹고 싶어요 = want to eat.
